speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: THE LATE MR. DONALD GORDON TRIBUTES TO DECEASED PUBLIC SERVANT AND INDUSTRIALIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house from my place that Mr. Donald Gordon, one of Canada's most distinguished public servants, died suddenly on Saturday. We are all well aware of his towering accomplishments as deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, chairman of the Foreign Exchange Control Board and, later, as chairman of the Wartime Prices and Trade Board. He was director of the Industrial Development Bank and, at the summit of his career, chairman of the board of directors and president of the Canadian National Railways from 1950 to 1966.
We have always regarded the late Mr. Gordon as the kind of person who personifies Canada abroad. He was large in stature and decisive in action. In his career we all have much to admire and learn. Following his appointment as president of Canada's largest railway, Mr. Gordon is reported to have said:
All my life I had learned things from the bottom up. Now I am learning from the top down and I find it's a lot harder.
From either direction Donald Gordon learned fast and learned well; and Canada benefited as a result. I am sure all hon. members will join with me in expressing sincere sympathy to Mrs. Gordon and the Gordon family.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: THE LATE MR. DONALD GORDON TRIBUTES TO DECEASED PUBLIC SERVANT AND INDUSTRIALIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the members of this party I join with the Prime Minister in expressing our regrets to the family of the late Mr. Gordon. We appreciate what he did for this country. There are not many people of whom it can be said genuinely that they were builders of the country. Mr. Gordon did his share of building as deputy governor of the Bank of Canada and as chairman of the board and president of Canadian National Railways. Earlier in his career he did good work as chairman of the Foreign Exchange Control Board and of the Wartime Prices and
Trade Board. His accomplishments earned him the gratitude of his country.
He was a big man; he was the kind of man this country needs and it was our good fortune that he came here from Scotland. We did not always agree with what he said, but we always respected him for the vigour and determination with which he pursued his ideas. We hope that condolences of the members of this party will be conveyed to Mr. Gordon's family.

maintopic: THE LATE MR. DONALD GORDON TRIBUTES TO DECEASED PUBLIC SERVANT AND INDUSTRIALIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party join with the Prime Minister in paying tribute to the memory of Donald Gordon, one of this country's great public servants who over a period of years did titanic work as head of the Foreign Exchange Control Board, chairman of the Wartime Prices and Trade Board, director of the Industrial Development Bank and chairman of the board and president of Canadian National Railways. For his work as president of Canadian National particularly this country is deeply indebted to him for his vision and for the vigour with which he discharged his responsibilities.
Although we did not always agree with him we could not help admiring the forcefulness with which he defended his ideas and the efficiency with which he carried out any task assigned to him. Here was a public servant who worked hard to do the job given to him by respective governments of this country. On behalf of this party I join with other hon. members in all parts of the house in expressing our deep sympathy to Mrs. Gordon and the Gordon family.

maintopic: THE LATE MR. DONALD GORDON TRIBUTES TO DECEASED PUBLIC SERVANT AND INDUSTRIALIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the leader of our party and of my colleagues, I should like to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the previous speakers to extend by deepest sympathy to the bereaved family of the late Donald Gordon.
Mr. Speaker, we mourn his death because Mr. Gordon was a great man who rose from the ranks to reach high positions in the government. As the Prime Minister said, his accomplishments in the service of his country and towards its development were towering. We extend our sincere sympathy to the bereaved family.

1.	In light of the severely restricted opportunities for employment of persons graduating from Canadian universities this year, will the government amend repayment provisions of the Student Loan Fund, to take account of the inability to repay of those students who cannot find jobs upon graduation?
2.	What other specific steps is the government taking to assist Canadian students who are graduating this year and are unable to find adequate employment?

speakeroldname: Mr. Yves Forest (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Finance and Manpower and Immigration as follows: 1. The regulations made pursuant to the Canada Student Loans Act provide for a large degree of flexibility in setting repayment terms. They are capable of accommodating virtually every conceivable situation, including cases where students are unemployed following graduation and cannot commence regular repayments immediately following the expiry of their interest and repayment free period. Borrowers are required, however, in all cases, to discuss their particular circumstances with the bank to which their loans are owed, before agreement can be reached on appropriate repayment terms.
2. As the number of graduates entering the labour force has increased, a proportionate increase of effort to assist their placement has been made by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Through 57 Canada Manpower Centres on various university campuses and in community colleges, students are being supplied with pertinent information on job opportunities and the labour market generally. A clearing system covering all 350 Canada

Manpower Centres assures that student applications for employment can, when required, receive a wide exposure to potential employers. A Directory of Canadian Employers who have expressed interest in hiring graduates has been published by the department and made available to students through the campus centres. Additional information regarding job vacancies is fed back from the Canada Manpower Centre network to the centres on campus. Officers at all centres are maintaining, and as needed, increasing their efforts to seek out every possible job vacancy through their employer contacts.
So that students will receive as much assistance as possible in choosing university courses with a better knowledge of labour market demands and job opportunities, Canada Manpower Centre staff are intensifying their efforts to supply career and labour market information through the school guidance system.

Did the studies of the quality of the water in the St. Lawrence River between Kingston and Cornwall, since 1965, reveal any danger to swimmers?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: APPLICATION OF QUOTA TO CANADIANS ENTERING U.S.
speechtext:
The studies carried out in the international section of the St. Lawrence river under the aegis of the International Joint Commission, since 1965, have been designed specifically to examine whether or not there is pollution being discharged on one side of the international boundary which is causing or is likely to cause a threat to health or property on the other side of the boundary. The studies were not conducted to assess the water quality in local areas near the points of discharge. The findings of the studies are currently being reviewed by one of the International Joint Commission's Advisory Boards on Water Pollution, with a final report to the Commission expected later this year.

1. Canada has taken part in the Eleventh Session of The Hague Conference on Private International Law which was held at The Hague from October 7 to 26, 1968. The Hague Conference normally meets every fourth year. On September 4, 1968, Canada was admitted as a member and its instrument of acceptance was transmitted on the 7th day of October. Due to its form of government, Canada has found it difficult up to that time to seek membership in the Conference.
2.	No agreements binding on the participating government are signed at these sessions but delegates agree to submit to the appreciation of their governments draft conventions. At the conclusion of the 1968 session the following draft conventions were thus signed: (1) Convention on the recognition of divorces and legal separations; (2) Convention on the law applicable to traffic accidents; and (3) Convention on the taking of evidence abroad in civil or commercial matters. These conventions have not yet been ratified. Decision as to their ratification must await the conclusion of studies now being made of their import.
3.	A decision as to the entering into discussion with the provinces concerning the implementation of the conventions, must await decision as to their ratification and as to the best procedure to engage into such discussion; these questions are currently under study.

The purpose of this consultation is to ensure that national plans formulated independently by each country are as compatible as is considered desirable and possible by both countries. The agreement does not provide for integrated planning, and the two countries retain national control over their own civil emergency plans.
4.	On the Canadian side the principle participants in the discussion on this matter were officials of the Canada Emergency Measures Organization and the Department of External Affairs. Other Canadian departments concerned with civil emergency planning were associated with these discussions. On the United States side the principle participants were officials of the Office of Emergency Planning, the Office of Civil Defense and the Department of State. The draft agreement was concurred in by the U.S.-Canada Civil Emergency Planning Committee, and subsequently approved by the Canadian Cabinet.
5.	The agreement does not provide for a joint emergency board, but rather provides for a joint committee designated the United States-Canada Civil Emergency Planning Committee. Its membership comprises, for Canada: the Director General, Canada Emergency Measures Organization; a representative of the Department of External Affairs; and for the United States: the Director, Office of Emergency Planning; the Director, Office of Civil Defense; a representative of the Department of State.

If ever abortion committees are established in hospitals, it is essential to do so only after a very judicious selection of members, and after due consideration of their personal and professional qualifications.

Mr. Speaker, I feel duty bound to support the amendment moved by the member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise), which reads as follows:
That Bill C-150, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Parole Act, the Penitentiary Act, the Prisons and Reformatories Act and to make certain consequential amendments to the Combines Investigation Act, the Customs Tariff and the National Defence Act, be amended by deleting paragraph (f) of sub-section 6 of clause 18 on page 44 and substituting therefor:
"(f) "therapeutic abortion committee" for any hospital means a committee, comprised of not less than two qualified medical practitioners and one gynaecologist, appointed by the board of that hospital and approved by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of the province concerned, for the purpose of considering and determining questions relating to terminations of pregnancy within that hospital."
The purpose of the amendment is to define the abortion committee and to have its membership approved by the College of Physicians and Surgeons. The amendment also stipulates that a gynaecologist must sit on the committee. For that reason, we ask that such a specialist be appointed to the therapeutic committee.
I believe the amendment is a very important one, in that it requires medical specialists in this field to be almost infallible, because the question at issue is the right of a foetus or a child in his mother's womb to live or die.
In support of my arguments, I should like to quote the testimony of Dr. Benoit Legare, a gynaecologist at St. Francois d'Assise Hospital in Quebec City, before the parliamentary committee on justice and legal affairs, on March 25, 1969. In the following words, the specialist expresses his concern:
Moreover, even if it were liberal enough, to find that where abortion laws have been liberalized-

Either by creating committees of specialists or others in several countries, according to the Journal of the American Medical Association, of April 1961,
-these laws have not changed the figures relating to criminal abortions at all.
Some years ago, you abolished the death penalty out of humanitarianism and so that fatal miscarriages of justice would be avoided. Physicians also consider with fear this infallibility conferred upon them by allowing them to decide whether or not an innocent and defenceless being has the right to live.
The legislator's prime concern is to protect the citizens through the laws he enacts. Therefore, it is normal for him to show the greatest concern for the most ill-favoured, the weakest, the weakest of us all, namely the foetus, which is already legally accepted in society since according to sections 338 and 608 of the Civil Code it is already entitled to inheritance rights.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
We therefore ask you to humbly strike the clause dealing with abortion from the omnibus bill, though it might be submitted later on, amended after consultation with the different medical circles in the country.
If, per chance, we do not reflect the opinion of the majority, we would request you to consider as essential that the advisory committees set up to that end, be accepted by the College of Physicians of the different provinces or by a national body such as the Canadian Medical Association.
Those words definitely prove that this medical expert was puzzled about the legislative proposal. He added, and I quote:
We do not question the good intentions of the legislators. That is why we wanted to get in touch with the legislators. Perhaps legislators hope, through this bill, to limit the untold number of illegal abortions which are now performed throughout the country. However, they should not have too great expectations since the bill is not sufficiently liberal to hope to achieve this.
For all those reasons, I suggest that it is advisable to support this amendment so that responsible specialists be made members of the committee and be the ones to decide whether or not the foetus should be destroyed.

Mr. Speaker, a few words only to tell the house that I am in favour of this amendment, although I already know that they will not carry much weight with those who have been instructed to pass the bill.
The responsibility of the therapeutic abortion committee is to protect the mother's life. In fact, all decisions will be taken by that committee. I do not like its name. It sounds like that of a committee of executioners deciding among themselves whether or not the victim should be put to death.
May 5, 1969

When people suffer from illnesses, especially from serious ones, the doctors consult each other on the advisability of operating. Two or three of them talk a person's case over. I have never heard that in serious cases just anybody was consulted.
Abortion is very grave since it means the suppression of life. It is extremely grave and, in my opinion, the advisory committee should be made up of experts, namely gynaecologists.
This is a rather good amendment. If I had been called upon to bring in one, I would have demanded two gynaecologists instead of one on the committee. But as I have said, the amendment is quite broad. It is simply asking that the therapeutic abortion committee of a hospital should comprise at least two qualified doctors and one gynaecologist named by that hospital's council.
If we carry things to the extremes-as they will be in certain circumstances, on account of the love of money-I cannot conceive of a gynaecologist, if two general practitioners make a majority decision, being able to impose his opinions. In such a serious case, which would be the responsibility of specialists, the committee should be made up of gynaecologists. A general practitioner is less qualified as regards abortion.
The paragraph of Bill C-150 that the amendment would change reads as follows:
"therapeutic abortion committee" for any hospital means a committee comprised of not less than three members each of whom is a qualified medical practitioner-
In order to be a qualified medical practitioner, one needs only to have taken a medical course and obtained a general medical science degree. In considering this amendment. We must examine the question thoroughly, so as to avoid the abuses and consequences of the passage of this bill.
As regards the prejudicial consequences of this bill, if the committee is allowed to make extreme decisions, all members received a few comments from the Alliance for Life, that I should like to quote:
To what extent are you ready to "liberalize" the Canadian legislation on abortion?
In the opinion of certain members, the government's present proposals may seem deceptively moderate. In fact, however, it appears that such transformations are only a first step.
To my mind, this paragraph of Bill C-150, in its present form, is only a first step and a

great one toward excessive liberalization of abortion. I continue quoting the comments:
In Colorado, for example, such a law has done much to increase the number of abortions in hospitals-without reducing the number of clandestine abortions.
They think that will reduce the number of clandestine abortions; yet there is proof to the contrary in the countries where abortion has been legalized. Moreover, it is only the beginning of the stampede. I go on quoting:
Some countries have adopted more permissive laws; they went as far as legalizing abortion at will.
It is what will happen if this paragraph is maintained. Quite naturally, this will lead to abortion at will. I continue quoting:
Most of them however have started by legalizing abortion for so-called reasons of health.
It is precisely what we say and what will be said by the members of this committee. It is likely that the pregnant woman can be sick. Likely, indeed. Let us say that three medical practitioners belong to the therapeutic abortion committee. This will not be the case in every hospital, but it is possible that committees of abortionists will be appointed. I have already spoken of it last week. So did Sweden In 1921. Later on, in 1938, abortion on social grounds ... and others became possible. In 1946, the law became still more permissive.

In Poland also, abortion was first legalized on vague "medical" grounds. In 1956, those grounds were extended to cover social reasons. Today, Polish laws on abortion are among the most permissive. in the world.

The first of those decisions was made in 1938 and since then, more and more pressure is being exerted in favour of abortion on request.
In my opinion, this bill, and especially the appointment of the committee, is paving the way to abortion on request. I am sure the

Criminal Code
minister is aware of it. For Canada, this is only a beginning where abortion and homosexuality are concerned. We made a first mistake by agreeing to the introduction of those two measures in the house.
I am entirely against the present wording of subclause (f) and I shall vote in favour of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Abitibi because it provides a means of ensuring the presence of a gynaecologist on this committee. I am sure that if the government accepted this amendment, it would be commended instead of being criticized.
He would at least have understood what kind of amendment to the Criminal Code the people want. He would have understood also that the population is against the massacre of innocents.
Mr. Speaker, I say again that our society is going to pass a legislation which will allow the most shameful acts a people could be guilty of. I am sure that we will have to pay some day for such acts and for this legislation that should never have been introduced.
I shall be brief, because I want to give the government and government members the opportunity to vote for their fine bill they love and cherish so much. However, I repeat that I shall feel duty bound, as a Roman Catholic and a human being, to vote against this bill which will allow every licence in the future.

Mr. Speaker, it must be stated specifically that the committee should be made up of competent gynaecologists, as stipulates this logical amendment intended to safeguard the life of human beings, to allow them to grow and develop normally.
In Canada, the population is not large enough for the debts we have to pay. Instead of turning to massive immigration, we should protect our population, allow it to increase at the rate Providence would have it. If the hospitals do not have competent committees, we will not reach the goal set by Providence.
Providence placed us in Canada and asked us to grow and multiply. The rules that are about to become law with regard to abortion cannot meet divine requirements. In Canada, the population should increase according to the views of Providence.
That committee should protect any being that is intended to live, that has the right to exist. I believe the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) would certainly be held in higher

esteem if instead of introducing such senseless rules as those on abortion, he suggested that an amount of at least $1,000 be given to every mother of a family who brings a child into the world. In so doing, we would accomplish an eminently human act, while enabling the family to develop.
The committee to be appointed should include a gynaecologist. In fact, such an important committee should include two gynaecologists, as the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) said.
I feel we should consider that logical amendment. I wonder why the minister of Justice does not intervene and approve this highly logical and commendable amendment.
It is time we tackled the amendments to the bill on abortion proposed by the government. Is the government truly concerned with the protection of a woman's life and health? If so, how can we be sure that the proposed amendments would achieve that purpose?
The committee whose establishment we recommend would be quite in a position to safeguard the health and the life of human beings. Never has the health of Canadians been as well protected as today. In Canada, the rate of maternal mortality is one of the lowest in the world, that is approximately three deaths out of 10,000 births. Can we really believe that the proposed amendments would bring an even greater improvement? The debate has failed to prove as yet that such an improvement would be ensured. It is rather surprising that nobody has raised that question yet. It is also significant that no doctor has shown that it would result in some benefit.
The committee we are proposing would take direct action to protect the human being, who-is so great and noble. If the human being did not exist, not much else would in this world.
We need such a committee and we want the assurance that the Minister of Justice supports this amendment. But he did not, and he is content with a status quo which is not good enough because it is beyond all bounds.
In Japan, abortion is legal and is granted: on request. According to the United Nations's statistics, the rate of maternal mortality in Japan is more than three times as high as in Canada.
Yugoslavia, which passed such a legislation, has a rate of maternal mortality more than four times as high as ours.
Can it be inferred that legislation making, abortion easier promotes health?
May 5. 1969



[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Canadians must provide themselves with committees made up of doctors of unquestionable ability.
Canada needs such committees and the services of gynaecologists in order to protect human beings and to ensure that all the requirements of our country are met. We would then thank Providence for protecting us from such acts of cruelty designed to reduce the population.
What we are doing today, every communist country has done before and I think that the legislation we are bringing forward is the most communistic and barbarous we have ever seen.
If various communist countries have committed such barbarous crimes, we do not have to imitate them. Since I do not believe the Minister of Justice is a communist, I am asking why he refuses to listen to our arguments in favour of those amendments.
The amendment now before the house is one of the most logical that has been moved. If we cannot avoid the barbarous acts that we are seeking to prevent through this Committee, the people would feel reassured if skilled men were to make such decisions. Those people, like the Minister of Justice, have been brought into the world to serve the population.
The gynaecologist and the other members of abortion committees must be highly qualified to ensure the protection of our nation. We must make sure that modern technology is made available as much as possible to every matter.
We need such committees and I do not see why the minister would deny society the presence of a gynaecologist on them. We have to sympathize with the Liberal member who lost his wife after refusing an abortion. The Canadian law cannot be blamed for it.
Let us keep in mind also that the tremendous advance of medicine since then has reduced the rate of maternal mortality from 10 to 1 in one generation. Medical authorities recognize that fact which is statistically proved. So it is ironical to claim that the amendments regarding abortion proposed by the government reflect the needs of our modern society.
What is the real purpose of that amendment? What is really going to be protected? Here are the comments of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), as reported on page 825 of the proceedings of the committee on
Criminal Code
health, welfare and social affairs, and I quote:
This is exactly what we want; to reduce any cause for perplexity in the legislation, mainly to protect the doctor.
Now, Mr. Speaker, since we had no such legislation in Canada and we were faring rather well, since medicine is more advanced I would say, than in several other countries, and since the number of deaths due to abortion in Canada is about 3 out of 10,000, we do not need a legislation such as the one brought in and I consider once again that the minister should at least be quite frank and tell us: I want the best, I want a committee to be set up. I do not believe the minister should oppose this amendment, which is a social, moral, human, and above all, life-protecting measure.
Then, why does abortion disturb people so much? If only the destruction of tissue, were involved, any objection to the proposed changes in the abortion legislation would seem quite inconsistent and irrational. Do we believe abortion merely destroys tissue? Is that what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Justice think?
Indeed, there are many who believe that abortion consists in getting rid of something similar to a blood clot.

Criminal Code
This unborn child even in the first few weeks is perfectly human, or is there anyone to pretend that it is a rat or a guinea pig?
Mr. Speaker, those reports show once again there is a great need tor the most logical and the most advisable committees. Members of such a committee should be highly respectable and have a wide knowledge of medical matters, since the decision to perform an abortion must be made by the most highly competent committee ever seen in the history of medicine.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We have those specialists. We only have to find them. We only have to bring them together and set up those committees. We shall then have at least a semblance of justice and be able to give the people related services, proficient services.
I believe that the Canadian people will have confidence in such a committee and I believe also that the mother, who has to go through this, will at least be sure of getting the proper care, thanks to such specialists. The mother surely has a right to life, and the child also. Such things must be protected, because they are the most natural, the most noble

Mr. Speaker, I fully support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) designed to specify how the famous committee appointed in every hospital will be set up.
I also support this amendment for several other reasons.
First of all, in places where therapeutic abortions are performed according to official statistics they are performed much more for questionable psychiatric reasons, and also with questionable results, than in order to save the mother's life. In fact, the bill on abortion compels us to ask ourselves whether we are ready to accept certain forms of murder.
According to the conclusions of a survey conducted by the Association of Quebec Hospital Medical Boards, the number of therapeutic abortions performed in the hospitals of the province is now very restricted and nil, in most cases.
Because of the very limited number of medical indications, the passing of the bill before

us would increase very little the number of therapeutic abortions; there would only be an increase in requests for abortion, with their dilemma.
Therapeutic abortion committees mentioned in that bill should only exist in hospitals having an adequate number of specialists and consultants in every branch, so that the decision may be the result of a just and unbiased judgment.
That inquiry-the report of the Association says so-revealed that most medical boards and boards of directors of Quebec hospitals officially and formally objected to the establishment of therapeutic abortion committees in their own hospital.
In view of professional ethics and the constant orientation of their profession, hospital doctors are very reluctant to be part of such committees, and moreover they personally refuse to perform any therapeutic abortion.
What would happen if one or more doctors refused to participate in the work of the abortion committee? Paragraph (f) of subsection 6 does mention "a committee of at least three members".
In view of the decisions taken by the said committee and the implications of such decisions for the committee members as well as for the patient, numerous questions come to mind.
Is it worth taking the risk of upsetting, by legislation, a state of balance arrived at in the status quo? Is it worth setting up a mechanism which could very well go beyond the intentions of the legislator?
Would it not be better to undertake a wider consultation open to all layers of the medical profession, to medical associations, specialists, etc.? Would it not be preferable to learn at this stage all the distinctions capable of improving the legislation even before it is adopted?
Amendment No. 20 of my hon. friend from Abitibi suggests that the said committee be made up of two doctors and one gynaecologist.
In every hospital, there are already research committees whose main aim is to improve medical practice and to allow consultation between specialists. In some hospitals, there are sometimes up to 10 voluntary committees.
However, the committee referred to in paragraph (f) of subsection 6 tends or aims to authorize the medical act. The terms used
May 5. 1969

Criminal Code
leave the door open to problems and to discussion. The main problem with therapeutic abortion committees is that psychiatrists, many of whom will accept any psychiatric indication, will ask gynaecologists to perform an abortion when the latter has refused to do it. This provision will also contribute to bargaining between female patients and their doctors.
Will the doctors and gynaecologists appointed by the hospital to form this abortion committee be working on a voluntary basis? According to a doctor's opinion, these voluntary committees and the work that would be assigned to them would not be considered as seriously as the measure suggests.
At this point, I am taking the liberty of quoting an extract from the proceedings of the committee on justice and legal affairs to show how the problem may be dealt with differently in each hospital.
In New York, an inquiry has been made in two hospitals located a few blocks from one another. It appears from this inquiry that in one of them there is one abortion per twenty deliveries and in the other, one per 6,000. Therefore, I think the proposed amendments would cause rather serious problems.
In the province of Quebec in particular, none of the small hospitals are interested in performing abortions. The doctors firmly believe that such accreditations are useless, a view that is supported by medical science itself. It should not be forgotten, besides, that the majority of Quebec doctors see no need for the proposed legislation or the institution of such committees.
As proposed, the institution of committees opens the door to all kinds of problems.
Psychiatric indications as grounds for abortion are rejected by the majority of doctors and psychiatrists. However, a few psychiatrists admit limited indications. We have to ask ourselves if, while amending the act and allegedly settling one problem, we are not creating another one.
Those are some of the reasons why doctors object to abortion.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There is also another aspect to be considered. What will be the position of physicians with regard to the committees created in the hospitals? Will they be compelled to comply with the decisions of the committee in the name of social order?
If the bill is passed in its present form, I expect two possible effects.
On the one hand, if the abortion committees strictly interpret the terms "the life or health" very few abortions will be allowed and the problem of illegal abortions will remain the same.
On the other hand, if the definition of the word "health" is somewhat broad, it will always be possible to find a reason to consider the pregnancy as dangerous.
A piece of legislation which lends itself to various interpretations and offers no more guarantees is incomplete.
Those are the reasons why I sincerely support the motion of the hen. member for Abiti-bi, the object of which is to strike out subsection (f) in paragraph 6 of clause 18 of the bill and to have it replaced by the amendment of the hon. member for Abitibi.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment I am sponsoring this afternoon is somewhat related to the amendment we have been discussing. It adds what I regard as an important dimension to this discussion in that it broadens the scope of interest and concern of those who will have the responsibility of making the very critical and vital decision when abortion shall take place.
One of the disturbing aspects of this long extended debate on the amendments to the Criminal Code, which has concerned me as well as many other hon. members and, judging from my mail, the majority of the people of Canada, is the direct antagonism expressed in some of the amendments to what has become known down through the centuries of western civilization as the Judaeo-Christian ethic. Up until fairly recent times, this century as a matter of fact, this has been the basis upon which our system of jurisprudence has been established; it has been largely the ethical and value basis upon which we have made moral decisions.
The amendment brings into abortion this vital question: Who will make the decision as to life or death with respect to a human individual? We know that the Judaeo-Christian ethic regards as of fundamental importance the value of an individual human life. My amendment brings into focus the advice of a psychiatrist. I think this is a very necessary and important dimension in a decision of this kind because the science, if I may use that term, of psychiatry has become pretty well established in the practice of the healing arts today. I shall be dealing with this matter later in my remarks.
But most important, where the individual wishes it the amendment makes it possible for the person concerned or, if it is a family problem, the family concerned, to call in a clergyman or spiritual adviser to deal with this vital and broader dimension in a life or death decision. I know that certain churches in this country have become quite concerned that we are moving toward a humanistic, secular, materialistic attitude toward life. Once the dikes are breached, of course, the value of individual life, as has been the experience in other countries where humanism is rampant, becomes constantly reduced until there are episodes, such as we recall within recent memory, of whole nations dedicated to the principle of genocide, the extermination of human life, because individuals or groups of individuals have been regarded as less than human and, like pests, should be
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
eliminated because they are no longer serving any useful function.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) has argued-and I hope I am not unfair in this statement-that legal matters of this kind do not have any moral overtones or moral implications; in other words, the law does not concern itself with questions of morality. If I am wrong in this respect, he can correct me when he enters the debate once again. It is my strong view that law is very firmly based on morality, particularly law as we understand it in western civilization. We used to call it western Christian civilization. Our law stems from the decalogue which, as we know, has strong moral and religious overtones. If the humanists want to say that law has no direct relationship to moral codes, I think even the sociologists would agree that it at least has some relationship to the mores. These patterns for human behaviour have moral overtones even though they are not as firmly based as those which have undergirded the common law and even our criminal law practice.
There is a fundamental shift taking place in this amendment and other amendments in that, instead of the relationship of man in his society being anchored to concepts that derive from our values which stem from our Judaeo-Christian traditions, it is shifting in the direction of humanistic moral relativism. When that happens in a society I think it is fair to conclude that we are entering into a moral morass and a sea of confusion. I believe-and my mail has testified to this fact-that the majority of Canadians are still on the side of a moral basis for our legal system. This is why I think the Minister of Justice should at least accept this attempt to preserve some of the traditions that have been a vital part of our civilization up to the present time. All it is doing is to add a spiritual dimension so that it will not only be medical doctors-after all, they are specialists trained in a very narrow field-who will make this life and death decision.
If we are going to use the law to change and shape the social order, I suggest we are moving in a dangerous direction. I spoke in this vein a week or so ago with reference to gross indecency, and some of the pundits referred to my comments as being social jingoism. This merely underlines the moral and social confusion rampant in our society when the values and traditions of our Judaeo-Christian civilization, with the experience of

centuries behind it are referred to as social jingoism.
It might be proper to ask at this stage how our society has become so deeply saturated and penetrated by the moral relativism that is indicated in some of this so-called reform legislation. I suppose that the chief sources of influence have been the academic scribblers of the last century, most of whom were concentrated in the last half of the 19th century. The press has popularized science or pseudoscience, and today the process goes on apace through the tremendous social impact of the mass media which have sometimes been referred to as chromium-plated madhouse generating myths, folklore and a reality of its own, a sort of instantaneous electronic folklore because it has no connection either with the past or with the future.
The chief architects of some of these ideas have been men like Darwin, Marx, Herbert Spencer and Freud. As one who has been through the process of higher education, both on the giving and the receiving line, I freely admit that the ideas which stem from these four gentlemen and many other academic scribblers of the last half of the last century have become the guiding stars and the intellectual illumination for much of contemporary society. Darwin gave us the theory of biological evolution, and Marx gave us the doctrine of political and economic expediency, sometimes called atheistic communism or scientific socialism.
Hear, hear.

I hear a "hear, hear" from across the way, but these are the terms that apply to these systems. We debate today whether God is dead or alive, but we forget that it was Marx who first explicitly stated in modern pseudo-scientific, social, jingolistic terms that God was quite definitely dead, and he gave us a political and economic system based on this thesis. Herbert Spencer combined biological evolution with humanism to produce his theory of social evolution or social Darwinism which said that in every way and every day we are getting better and better. Of course this was not borne out by the events of the first half of the 20th century.
I have given credit to psychiatrists already so I must not depart from that thesis, but Freudian psychology and the Freudian interpretation of human behaviour have strongly saturated our society. Someone has described a Freudian psychologist as the odd examining 29180-5272

the id, and there may be some truth in that description.
Science, or perhaps I should say pseudoscience, has become a sacred cow, and belief in progress because of human perfection has been accepted almost universally, at least in institutions of higher learning.
I recall that Harold Innes, who was a great puncturer of academic balloons until recent times at the University of Toronto, called this process the new mysticism. I think that was a very apt description of the system. It is sometimes referred to as Fabianism or the inevitability of the perfect man, man in his natural state breaking through the corruption of his social institutions and achieving a peace and perfection out of the process of change that is going on apace in society. Perhaps I should resort to doggerel to simplify it so that he who runs may read. I came across this little poem which oversimplifies but which I think expresses the thought. It goes as follows:
Man used to be a tadpole learning how to swim, And then he was a frog with his tail tucked in. And then he was a monkey hanging from the tree. And now he is a professor with a Ph.D.
His strength is as the strength of ten because he has taken 600 hours in social science and he knows all there is to be known about everything. He is omniscient and omnipotent and is exercising all the functions that we used to attribute to God.

To come back to the point I wish to make, which I think is a vital one, these trends marked by the new social jingoism that I have outlined briefly this afternoon inevitably result in social and political action. This is exactly what is happening in this legislation. The ideas of creative individuals in society, the academic scribblers, eventually penetrate down through society to our social institutions and are implemented in the form of social and political action.
Legislation has been brought before this house, as I have already indicated, that is not based on values enshrined within our Judaeo-Christian past but is an attempt to shape our society in terms of the new secularism, humanism and materialism. This is the motivating principle behind the legislation with which we are confronted at the present time.
If we carry this through to its logical conclusion, it results in some of the episodes that are a blot on 20th century civilization. The Nazis, those madmen in authority, without a

Until this century social change involved man changing his environment for the general benefit of man. We are now moving into a new, more critical and dangerous area of man changing himself in biological terms in order to adjust to his environment. This was first predicted by Aldous Huxley in his "Brave New World", when by means of pseudo-scientific and test tube methods he first satirically conceived of the possibility of biological engineering as contrasted to social engineering.
When the Nazis came to power in that great civilized nation of Germany, they introduced a master race theory that was based on the misapplication of the science of eugenics, hoping thereby to produce a generation of supermen. I am right on the button here, Mr. Speaker. As I said in my opening remarks, I am introducing the new dimension of inviting a clergyman or spiritual adviser to consult on this question of life or death. I am indicating exactly how we have reached the present situation where we are negating what used to be a vital and fundamental part of our western society. With great respect to Your Honour, it is within this background that I think it is necessary to make this particular point. However, I am almost at the end of my remarks.
Our own society is deeply saturated with these new values, and they have a devastating impact on basic social institutions, which we know are the family, institutions of education, the church and the state. Had I time this afternoon I would perhaps have gone into this matter a little more. We all know that social and moral confusion is rampant in our own society as well as in many other parts of the western world, and this confusion is directly related to some of these pseudo-scientific

notions. This social jingoism has so saturated our society that it has become the motivating principle behind our own pattern of life without our hardly being aware of it.
What this amendment is asking, Mr. Speaker, is that at least we nostalgically recognize that there are dimensions other than the purely physical, that the members of the therapeutic abortion committee examine more than the physical and medical problem. Certainly we should make obeisance to the science of psychiatry and bring such a gentleman into consultation on this important matter, because he does add a psychological dimension. More especially, where the patient so desires, she should have the right to request the attendance of a clergyman or a spiritual adviser.
We now recognize the psychosomatic dimension. In the science of medicine, therapy involves the treatment of the whole person. If we are going to avoid some of the harsher aspects of the amendment that is being proposed by the government, we should at least recognize that we are talking not just of a physical and a medical problem. I am sure that those of us who have been involved in social work know from personal knowledge and experience that abortion, concerning as it does human life, leaves deep-rooted psychic and spiritual scars that are often not healed no matter what therapeutic approach is taken later.
Therefore I urge without further words that the minister accept this amendment, that he at least recognize and acknowledge that while we are moving in a dangerous, new direction in our outlook toward the nature of man and society, we are nevertheless looking nostalgically to the past and admitting that what has gone on in the past in terms of our Judaeo-Christian approach to life has not been entirely wrong.

And acquiring the added virtue of patience. What the amendment of the hon. member strives to do is to make specific provision for the membership of the therapeutic abortion committee. When the bill went through the committee stage before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs the government, and I on behalf of the government, considered over 30 amendments and accepted about 25. What we are dealing with is the committee's report at the report stage of the proceedings. Our position will once again be that we accept the committee report and accept even those parts of it that went against the government's position. Since we accept the report I am afraid I must recommend to the house that we reject the hon. member's amendment. I shall try to explain why.
Under proposed section 237 (6)(f), as contained in clause 18 of the bill, the requirement is that a committee such as is here being considered shall consist of not less than three duly qualified medical practitioners. Subsection 4(c) of section 237 involves purely medical considerations. We argue that the make-up of the therapeutic abortion committee ought to be that of medical practitioners. The therapeutic abortion committee must by certificate in writing state that in its opinion the continuation of the pregnancy of a female person would or would be likely to endanger her life or health. That appears to be a medical decision. It is a medical assessment of whether the life or health of the mother is endangered. The doctors must assess whether her life or health is endangered. That being so, there appears no justification for having persons on the committee who do not have the necessary training and qualification to serve on it. In other words, members of the committee must have medical training and medical qualifications.
The hon. member's motion speaks of a psychiatrist. One can conceive of a great many cases where a woman seeking an abortion is doing so because of a heart or a kidney condition or some other physical ailment. There is no need for psychiatric help in such circumstances. Such matters are best left to hospital boards. It is our position that in establishing these committees hospital boards ought to be given as much flexibility as possible in order that they may make use of all available medical expertise needed to pronounce upon the life or health of the person involved.

The hon. member also suggested that a clergyman ought to be a member of the therapeutic abortion committee. Here again I say to him that the decision to be made by the committee is a medical decision. That does not stop a woman from seeking spiritual help.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But there is nothing to bar a woman from consulting her own spiritual adviser before she sees the doctors. She can consult her spiritual adviser about the moral decision involved in order to assess her moral position before she approaches any doctor or hospital. So far as I am concerned I would encourage a woman faced with such a problem to obtain whatever spiritual advice and guidance she may to assist her own judgment and conscience. But having done that and having decided she wants an abortion, she then comes under the terms of this proposed section. The judgment whether continuation of the pregnancy will affect the life or health of the mother is a medical judgment, and I say that prior to seeking medical advice the woman is entitled at all times to consult her own spiritual adviser. I encourage her to do so. But, with the greatest respect, a spiritual adviser cannot contribute to the medical judgment contemplated by the clause.
Practitioners of psychosomatic medicine would not agree with that.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to avail myself of the few remaining minutes to support the amendment of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). I think this amendment is logical and goes to the heart of the matter. We are about to pass a bill which will have very serious consequences, as it affects the very basis of human nature. It is as the root of the tree. If we want the tree to be in good condition, in good health, we must take care of its roots. If the roots become sick, the tree will die. If the nation is in danger, if the very basis of the nation is undermined, it will be the fault of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), the fault of the government. This bill might shake them. I believe that we should recognize that this amendment is moral, logical, social and that it must not be rejected on any ground.
This amendment should be accepted because the one who moved it deserves all our congratulations. I am asking the hon. member, once again, if it is possible, to ask his friends to support his amendment because up to now only one member has supported it.
This amendment certainly deserves a lot of support, because it carries a lot of weight. Moreover, it is so logical, so moral, so social, that I think it is impossible not to take it into account.
The Minister of Justice said in his statements, that he was ready to advise mothers to turn to a spiritual advisor, a moralist, a psychiatrist. If the minister is ready to do that, why does he not include it in his bill?
The minister stated publicly that he was ready at least to recognize that this amendment is logical. Why not include it in the bill and have it inserted in the Criminal Code? After a bill has been passed, it comes into force and then that legislation is maintained by the State. If that amendment does not appear in the Criminal Code, those who have to enforce the law will not bother about it. Therefore, the minister implies only that the
May 5, 1969

amendment, though logical and commendable, cannot be accepted.

Mr. Speaker, before recess we were discussing an amendment which I called just and tremendously great.
That amendment is more complete than any of the preceding ones, because it asks for, and I quote:
-not less than four members, two of whom shall be Qualified medical practitioners and one a psychiatrist appointed by the board of that hospital, as well as a clergyman, or spiritual advisor where this is requested by the patient for the purpose of considering and determining questions relating to terminations of pregnancy-
Mr. Speaker, as this question deals with morals, since it is impossible to appeal to conscience without touching morals, I should like to say a few words and broaden the outlook on the question of morality. Indeed, it is the greatest, the noblest thing, since morality ensures our inner balance and nurtures hope. It is the same thing for the population as a whole.
Since the population is made up of individuals, if we can preserve in each person the sense of morality, on the human and social plane, society itself will be stabilized, thanks to this morality, to this fundamental moral law needed by every man. Without such a law, no person is stable. Therefore, a nation without morality is an unstable nation heading for anarchy and ruin. No morality means no hope.
This is partly why this amendment, tending to allow the patient to request a spiritual advisor seems to me essentially logical, human, and commendable, for I will say it again, moral laws are essential to any nation.
Criminal Code
We must withdraw contemporary societies from the influence of artificial, legalistic rules and bring them into the vivifying world of duty and moral obligation. So we have a moral obligation to protest against this bill, because this is a matter of conscience.
Never before, I believe, has Parliament been faced with such a matter of conscience. Those who have no conscience, who follow like sheep, who let themselves be lead to the slaughterhouse, we cannot blame them, neither can we blame those who have a conscience, who wish to upgrade the nation, who want to ennoble the human being, who wish to protect individuals, to protect the nation, and who are against anarchy.
We are against anarchy and the legislative proposals on which we are to vote will surely and definitely lead us towards anarchy, because nations that have adopted similar legislation, similar positions, have known anarchy, have lived in terrible anarchy.
Every society and every nation should then be ruled by the same basic law: the respect of man. That is what I am driving at. The respect of man for man and of the state for the individual is at the very root of the social and human order.
Now, this amendment leads us directly into such moral considerations. It makes us turn our minds to morality for the protection of our society, for its very survival, and for its development and its future growth. We need such a high moral law.
Order postulates a law which sets a goal and which requires means to attain that goal. In nature, goal and means blend into one, because things and people are subjected to a vigorous determination. Whether it be the physical universe, the vegetable or animal kingdom, the goals and the means are summed up in the universal law of self-conservation and of respect for man.
A society established on the principle of respect of man must not confuse the end and the means. The state must not embody the end as well as the means. It is impossible to be both instrument and purpose and that is precisely what the present government is proposing now. It brings forth the instrument, while the purpose of the bill before us is to make abortion currently and generally obtainable and to remove all scruples about abortion. That is exactly what makes abortion so valuable, because once more it is concerned with the very essence of individuals, of life and of the human beings who

May 5. 1969
Criminal Code
will come after us. We shall not live forever and after we have been replaced things may be better. After our times, new, better, perhaps more sociable and natural things will come up because of our accomplishments, and if we have misbehaved, we will pay for it in the other world.
In our society, the role of the State is to legislate and to administer the law. It is up to the State not to embody at the same time-it must not do so by a strict application of the law-the end and the finality of society, that is to be enclosed in a specific institution. It is therefore necessary for the basic law of the human society to be embodied in a specific institution which would hold the supreme power above the State and out of its reach.
The motion under consideration leads us directly once again to a matter of conscience and ethics. It also shows that it is necessary to put that institution out of the reach of the State. A moral law is powerless in itself. It would be too easy for the State to abolish it or to violate it to its own advantage if it felt like it. Of course, the State always and necessarily has authority since it is in power. Then, having regard to that power, what will the Minister of Justice do?
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The minister acknowledges that the bill must be based on morals, but he does not want morals to be part of the Criminal Code. He does not want such a written law. Then, what are we to think of the minister? What about that Minister of Justice? Perhaps he should be called the Minister of Injustice, for he advocates or accepts certain reforms or certain moral laws only in principle, whereas he actually refuses to accept them.
So, such a minister reflects supernatural hypocrisy; it is not even natural hypocrisy. The basic law of society must not be violated by anybody and above all by the State. If everything is relative as far as humanity is concerned, in this case this is an absolute imperative. Otherwise, all would be lost.
Mr. Speaker, just as the means must be subordinated to the end, so the State must be subordinated to moral power. This is natural and necessary in the order of things. There is no denying this, Mr. Speaker.
Embodying the supreme law of the nation, the moral power must be a real power. Life is not sufficient. It must have moral power and not material power. The only real immaterial power is justice. Moral power and judiciary power must be one power only.
[Mr. Latulippe.l
However, this becomes a matter of conscience, Mr. Speaker.
The amendment now under study should certainly be accepted by a great many hon. members, by the hon. members on the other side of the house, by those who, up to now, have refused to accept any amendment to this bill.
And yet, the amendment under consideration is one of the most complete, most human, and most social-minded ever seen. So, humanity will be what man makes of it. Man harvests what he sows. Therefore, if he spreads disorder in our society, if he prevents society from multipling itself by immoral laws, like the one we are now considering, we shall be subjected to dreadful calamities.
As far as I am concerned, I shall not take that responsibility. If the minister and members opposite want to accept such a responsibility, they can do so. We are here as conscientious objectors. We want peace and happiness for the nation. We want the nation to progress; we want to be replaced by others who are logically supposed to replace us according to the destiny of creation. And, we have no right to interfere with such things.
The world that is dying under our very eyes is that of ideologies, objections, myths, of right supported by force, of false values or false ideologies; when in contact with reality, these degenerate into material values.
People consider only the material point of view, for they do not care for the spiritual point of view. They do not care about morals. There are no more morals, there is no more conscience on the other side at the present time. However, I feel that all government, members cannot be deprived of a conscience.
Among our friends opposite, some are still conscientious. I ask them to stand up and defend the bill, so that we can at least have that logical, great and ultimate amendment adopted.
That amendment should at least be inserted in our Criminal Code, so as to provide some measure of protection, a little conscience, a little hope, for our nation, today and tomorrow.
The world of quality and of masses, the world of all those who, avid for power or money built their empire on the traffic of men, of their flesh, of their mind, of their conscience or of their faith, the world of the ignored, despised, crushed man, used as an instrument, the world of pride, of violence, of fanatism and of war, is an inhuman world.
May 5, 1969

Therefore, this is what we are in the process of giving the people, the future nation: an inhuman world. Yet we were not elected to indulge in inhuman things. We are human beings and so, we must know what is moral, what is a human being, an individual. We must recognize its greatness, its sublimity.
So, the break of dawn, the new-born world will be the world of reality and of living men, the world of genuine human values, both material and spiritual. That is what we want, that is what we stand for, with this bill and with the amendment proposed in it. The world of quality is the world of the elite, of all those who, on this earth, are the most worthy of our times, in short the world of moral law, of tolerance and of peace. It is the world of the man who is understood, considered, respected, treated as a human being, the world of the happy city, built by free men for free men who are masters of their own destiny.

Mr. Speaker, we are studying, clause by clause, the amendments which have been introduced in this house concerning bill C-150.
Some similar amendments have been tabled previously, but we must still express our views on each of these amendments which are, I think, very important.
If we have a close look at the amendment No. 30, introduced by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) we notice that it is rather similar to the previous one. We sincerely regret that the minister does not seem willing to accept any of those amendments which were not been moved for fun, or for mere pleasure.
Each of them is important if one takes trouble to study the documents, the briefs, to read the medical books and to learn from the experience of other countries which have already enacted such bills.
The main purpose of this amendment is to clarify in bill C-150 the wording of the provision which compels us to appoint abortion committees where this wording would specify in advance the members who would be appointed to these abortion committees.
Now, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris suggested that a psychiatrist be appointed with two doctors and a clergyman of the religion or the belief of the female person who wants to have an abortion. Well, the main
Criminal Code
purpose of this amendment is to specify in the legislation who within the abortion committee, will have the final say from the psychiatric point of view.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Why should there be a psychiatrist on this committee? Because medical science proves that in the case of abortion a psychiatrist is very important because of the many psychiatric symptoms which induce women to go to certain doctors to get an abortion.
How could a doctor study the reason a woman has to want an abortion if he is not himself a psychiatrist? I have here, in front of me, books written by doctors who give hundreds of psychiatric reasons for which a woman might want to get an abortion.
The legislation does not specify anything; it does not oblige the hospital board to have a psychiatrist on this committee. That is where we find the legislation is not clear enough, it is incomplete, ambiguous, it will open the door to a lot of abuses.
I am shocked to see that the minister is stubborn to the point that he will not accept any of the amendments proposed in the house.
Mr. Speaker, I simply have to mention the books published on the subject by doctors, books sold by the Editions du jour and written by Dr. Serge Mongeau, in collaboration with other doctors. Speaking of psychiatric conditions, he says this, at page 45, about unwanted pregnancies. He emphasizes cases where the psychiatrist alone could tell if such or such a woman is right or wrong to get an abortion.
Unwanted pregnancies
That reluctant approach can appear at the very beginning, for instance in the case of the bachelor girl who cannot foresee any way of keeping her child.
Further he is more specific:
Except in some very rare exceptions, the majority of women appear to be more or less in two minds when pregnant. At times the child is seen as a threat, at times as the object of tender love. The psychological state of the woman, her environment, her health, her relations with her husband, all condition her attitude towards the child she bears.
Those are some psychiatric reasons- and I shall enumerate others-which induce a woman at the start of her pregnancy to either want or reject her child. Statistics prove, however, that a woman who wanted to be aborted because she did not want her child, later on, after one, two or three months,
Criminal Code had changed her mind and from then on wanted to bring her child into the world.
Mr. Speaker, those are psychiatric reasons for which a woman wants to be aborted or not. How are those psychiatric reasons to be judged if there is no psychiatrist on the committee?
Dr. Soddy, another expert in the field of psychiatry, has this to say:
Soddy distinguishes two forms of non-wish, in the face of pregnancy: "the absence of a positive desire for the child for his own sake, as an individual with his own rights; a negative attitude towards the child or even his rejection". Depending on the category, the character of the mother-to-be, the social possibilities and numerous other factors, four alternatives can be considered:
He goes on to explain, for instance, why a woman may finally accept her child, even though she may in the first instance have rejected it and wanted to be aborted, because the psychiatrist convinced her to have the child.
I continue:
Even when the discovery of pregnancy has caused the future mother to be slightly dismayed, it can happen, particularly when she receives adequate help, that the child who was first regarded as undesirable becomes fully accepted. In Yugoslavia, where abortion is legal if approved by a committee created to study the requests, this intervention is refused to 10 to 20 per cent of the women who request it. In 1960-61, an inquiry revealed that out of 762 women who had not been granted an abortion, 52.5 per cent in 1960 and 42 per cent in 1961 carried their pregnancy to its term. Out of that number, 92 per cent accepted their child normally-
And women who had first asked for an abortion, were convinced with advice and help from the psychiatrist on the abortion committee, to carry their pregnancy to its term. However, how can the doctors on the abortion committee judge the psychiatric reasons a woman may invoke for having an abortion, if they are not psychiatrists themselves? Therein lies the illogical and nonsensical attitude of the minister regarding the scientists, medical authorities in Canada who have submitted briefs, who have given us everything we need to draw up legislation which will meet fully the needs of the public, of the pregnant women, and of those desiring abortion.
We believe, he goes on to say, that it is necessary to try everything to motivate women to want maternity and through effective help, to make maternity acceptable to them as soon as possible. Social workers play an increasingly successful role in the special centres established for that kind of work.

May 5, 1968
But how can we convince the women who want an abortion for psychiatric reasons if there are no psychiatrists on the abortion committee? How can doctors who know nothing about psychiatry say: Madam, for such and such a reason, you should continue your pregnancy to term. That shows that our legislation is absolutely senseless and unsuitable for the Canadian people.
I would like to give another reason, a psychiatric one, put forward by a woman who wants an abortion. What can a doctor who is not a psychiatrist decide about that? Here is the case:
I am pregnant. I want an abortion but I can find nobody to do it; the only one who would be ready to do it charges $600, but I do not have that money. I cannot wait any longer; I will do it myself. My mind Is made up.
That is a woman who could surely be psychiatrically treated.
-I will use a knitting needle. It is dangerous,
I know; I risk a lot, I know; but I cannot do otherwise. Why do doctors let a person destroy herself? You help those who want to commit suicide, but you incite people to kill themselves perhaps. Is that human?
Isabelle, 20 years old.
Here is another psychiatric case which shows another reason why someone wants an abortion.
I think that in any case, if a woman wants an abortion, she finds the means to get it. And in what conditions?
Having myself had that experience, I can assure you that the steps you have to take, the refusals you have to suffer, fear and everything, are causing as much traumatism as the abortion itself. If abortion was allowed, with some restrictions, of course, there might be fewer serious consequences, physical as well as mental.
A single woman, 27 years old, Montreal
That is a riding represented by a Liberal member in this house, and not a single Liberal member has spoken for or against this proposed legislation. And the article goes on to say:
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I have known two "professional" abortionists. The first one: two girls died after abortions; he was acquitted for the first one but for the second one he got eight months in Bordeaux, plus $11,000 costs.
The second one: a girl died and her nude body was found in the alley of Drolet Street about 10 years ago. He was indicted; he got away without a prison sentence, thanks to his money ... He told me that about 50 per cent of the girls who think they are pregnant-

May 5, 1969

And here we come to the psychiatric point.
-50 per cent of the girls who think they are pregnant are not and in those cases he uses some red liquid and chicken liver that, after being dipped in the liquid, looks much like a foetus. When he had a new customer he sent a chauffeur to get her and who would then get him in a hospital lobby, and this patient believed he was a doctor. He aborted 20 girls or women per week. The price varied from $200 to $300. He gave $25 to anybody who brought him a good customer.
That was a long time ago; nowadays it goes much faster.
But, Mr. Speaker, if we look at the statement of this girl and the reason why she wanted an abortion, again we find psychiatric reasons. In the bill introduced by the minister there is no guarantee that a psychiatrist will be appointed. The minister does not want to accept psychiatric indications which would allow a woman, whether she is right or wrong, to decide whether or not she will go to a psychiatrist.
I will add here that there are other reasons, and I have many more:
If I hope that abortion will be allowed, it is because it is an obsolete, hypocritical and irrealis-tic legislation; it is also for the rich and not for the poor.
Wife of an unemployed worker in Mont-Laurier, 36 years old.
Mr. Speaker, further on we are also told that abortions vary according to each hospital. And yet, it is more or less the same people, the same women, the same diseases, the same psychiatry, the same pediatry, the same foetuses that are born.
The proportion of therapeutic abortions varies ... according to each hospital.
And in the United States, Mr. Hall, who has made a survey of those problems in various hospitals, says this:
Hall counted in one hospital one abortion out of 20 deliveries and in another none out of 24,417 deliveries.
It is estimated, generally speaking, that there are about 100 illegal abortions for every therapeutic abortion, and that illegal abortions are the cause of great medical risks for the mother's health or life.
And from the point of view of psychiatry too.
Further, when we are told how the committees are formed, we may wonder who the members are. Here is what is said about the committees.
The woman herself must make an application to secure a legal abortion. A special abortion committee within the Royal College of Medicine, a committee composed of a physician usually an obstetrician-
Criminal Code
-or a gynaecologist. The law does not mention a gynaecologist. Beside that gynaecologist-
-of an ordinary citizen, preferably a woman-
It would be normal that a woman should decide on the fate of another woman, of a person of the female sex, such as the one who wants an abortion, it would be normal that a woman conversant with that matter should be on the committee.
I carry on:
-and of the head of the Social Psychiatry Board, has to determine the value of the indications to decide for mentally retarded women and to appoint doctors who will be able to decide themselves whether they should perform an abortion. Those doctors, officially appointed, will be able to decide whether an abortion should be performed, if their decision is supported by another doctor, the one who usually performs the abortion.
In the present legislation, we are not told that the doctor who is to perform the abortion will be on the committee. A doctor may decide on the abortion and another doctor, who will have no decision to take on the case, will have to perform the abortion or the murder.
Mr. Speaker, in Denmark, where they like to speak about other countries, they say, and I quote:
-the legislation provides . . . "that a woman can obtain a miscarriage in special cases where physical or mental troubles-
Further on, they specify who is to be members of the hospital committees in Denmark, and I quote again:
-three members' appointed by the Department of Social Affairs. Two of them are doctors and one must be a specialist in psychiatry-
A specialist in psychiatry! Denmark requests only a psychiatrist and a general practitioner. In addition, it is said, and I am still quoting:
-the third member of the committee is always the director of an agency . .. called "Assistance to the mother".
The minister proposes a legislation on abortion but he does not intend to set up committees of "Assistance to the mothers". He suggests the establishment of abortion committees, but not committees to assist the mother. Nothing is said in this respect. There is no mention of it in the legislation while in a country like Denmark, committees have been established to help the mother. Why? Because a woman is refused an abortion for psychiatric reasons. At the same time, she is referred to a psychiatric committee to help here reach her term.

I have in hand a very interesting table on this subject, Mr. Speaker. Who knows today, in the world as elsewhere, what are the main reasons why abortions are requested? It is for the same reasons that we, of the Creditiste party, say that to want to allow abortion in Canada for health reasons is a false pretext. Such reasons do not exist.
Here are some figures:
In Yugoslavia, for instance, in 1965, here are the reasons why abortions were requested: 23 per cent of the women who secured an abortion have done so, not for reasons of health but of housing.
The Canadian government is not solving anything now and the minister responsible for housing has been compelled to resign because the government would not accept his views nor his proposals.
In Yugoslavia, Mr. Speaker, 23 per cent of the women who have asked for an abortion have done so because of lack of housing; 30 per cent, for economical and social reasons, because they did not have enough money to live. Moreover, 16 per cent of them have invoked family relationships; 6 per cent, illness in the family, but not their own; 3 per cent, marital relationships; 4 per cent, alcoholism; 9 per cent, various reasons, of a personal nature, and 2 per cent, various other reasons.
Well, this means that in Yugoslavia, 95 per cent of the women have secured an abortion for reasons completely different than those invoked in Canada to legalize abortion.
